title: The Debug Lab
description: Four broken robots, symptoms only. This is the single most valuable skill this course can leave you with: working backwards from what's wrong to why.

content.value: A real robot doesn't announce what's wrong with it. It just behaves strangely, and the person building it has to reason backwards: what would have to be true, physically or in the code, to produce exactly this symptom and no other?

Every category below traces back to something this course already taught. Power failures connect to Module 3. Wiring failures connect to Modules 4 through 8. Sensor failures connect to Module 7. Code failures connect to Modules 9 and 10.

content.title: 🔍 Diagnose each robot
content.prompt: Read each symptom and decide which category the fault is really in.

tasks.label: Both motors are commanded at the same speed, but the robot drives in a slow circle instead of straight
tasks.explain: If both motors are truly told to spin the same speed, a circle almost always means one motor's leads are swapped — it's spinning backwards relative to the other, cancelling out forward progress on that side.

tasks.label: The status LED blinks exactly as programmed, but the wheels never turn at all
tasks.explain: A working LED proves the controller has power and is running your code correctly. Something between the controller's output pins and the motor driver is disconnected — a wiring problem, not a power or code one.

tasks.label: robot.distance() always returns 0, no matter what's actually in front of the robot
tasks.explain: A reading that never changes at all, regardless of the real world, points straight at the sensor itself — miswired, facing the wrong way, or physically blocked.

tasks.label: The whole robot resets and reboots the instant the motors start spinning
tasks.explain: Motors draw a big current spike when they start. If that spike drags the shared voltage rail down far enough, the controller can brown out and reset — a classic power-system symptom, not a code bug.

tasks.label: The robot reliably turns left every single time the code says right
tasks.explain: Nothing here is physically wrong — the hardware does exactly what it's told. The instruction itself is simply backwards somewhere in the program.

content.value: Notice the method: rule things out by what still works. A blinking LED rules out total power failure. A distance reading that changes at all (even wrongly) rules out a fully dead sensor. Debugging is mostly the art of finding what's still working, and narrowing from there.

Key takeaway: diagnosing a fault means reasoning backwards from a symptom to its likely cause — and every category of fault (power, wiring, sensor, code) traces back to a specific part of this course you already understand.

quiz.question: A robot's status LED works perfectly, but the motors never respond. What does the working LED tell you?
options: The controller has power and is running code correctly, ruling out a total power failure
quiz.explain: A working LED is strong evidence the controller itself is fine — it narrows the fault to something downstream of the controller.

quiz.question: Why does a motor-triggered reset point at the power system rather than the code?
options: It's a coincidence with no real explanation
Motors draw a current spike on startup that can sag shared voltage below the controller's minimum, causing a brownout reset
Resets are always caused by bad code, never by hardware
quiz.explain: This is a genuine, common real-world failure mode — a physical, electrical cause producing a symptom that could easily be mistaken for a software bug.

quiz.question: What's the general debugging strategy this lesson teaches?
options: Reason backwards from the symptom, using what still works correctly to rule out entire categories of fault
Always assume the code is at fault first
quiz.explain: Using what's still working to eliminate possibilities is the real, transferable skill — far more useful than any specific fix.
